title: Show HN: VODForge – a free local desktop UI for YouTube video/playlist downloads
author: coopernusbaum

raw.text:
I built VODForge because I work with a CTV company that needed to pull YouTube videos from our channel partners into our media workflow.

Converter sites are always an option but the bitrate wasn't optimal for a CTV network that needs to make multiple streaming version off of a single source file. So I build vodforge to use yt-dlp and ffmpeg under the hood with preconfigured settings for the highest quality end result, automatically adjusting the output settings based on source quality, frame rate, and things like that.

It became a game changer internally for us because we were able to avoid sketchy converter sites and avoid paid converter software. Eventually I decided to release it for free and others loved it as well. We started to add support for many of the features that other software charges for, supporting 4K, playlist support, customizing application theme, persistent searchable library, auto organizing downloads by channel and playlist, MP3 support up to 320 kbps, and much more.

Looking for feedback on the user experience and additional features that you might find useful. My goal is to grow VODForge into a widely adopted free tool for people who do not want to deal with sketchy websites, CLI mess, or pay for things that you could ultimately do for free given time and effort. VODForge wants to make it EASY and maintained for you. We know anyone can make a GUI wrapper, but that is a trivial way to describe what VODForge aims to offer, user-friendliness, "it just works", libraries and packages maintained for you. All you should think about is what to download next.

VODForge awaits...

title: Show HN: HexBOTs – a cellular automaton with robotic lawnmowers
author: unitX

raw.text:
Double-click or press N to start a new experiment.

I built hexBOTs, an unusual cellular automaton based on deterministic robots.

The robots behave a bit like robotic lawnmowers, moving through their environment and reacting according to their individual rules.

The robots themselves are fully deterministic — no random functions are used while they are running. What makes them different is their “genetics”: each robot's behavior is defined by a randomly generated genome, which allows for an enormous number of different robot types.

Randomness creates the robots, but it doesn't drive them.

Once an experiment starts, everything follows deterministically from the generated genomes and the initial state. What fascinates me is the complexity that emerges from these relatively simple machines interacting with each other and their environment.

Controls:

B — enable/disable robots (also: hold mouse/finger down)

R — restart

N — new experiment (also: mouse/finger double-click)

D — save as picture

I — show information / controls
raw.title: Show HN: HexBOTs – a cellular automaton with robotic lawnmowers

Maybe I'm showing my age a bit, but I recall hearing that images should be saved in formats based on their type to save on file size. So, photographs would be JPEGs, illustrations and icons would be PNGs, vector images would be SVGs, etc.

But now it feels like no-one does this anymore. Every site I've seen just seems to store all images as webp now, with many outright uploading multiple megabyte photo files in PNG format. There also doesn't seem to be a lot of care put into uploading images that match the dimensions needed for the largest device either, with even tiny GIFs on sites like Discord often being full-sized images dozens of megabytes in size.

So, did the internet just decide that bandwidth and image sizes aren't a concern anymore? Did everyone just accept that every image is posted to one of the same 3 services and that everyone has a high-speed internet connection now?

title: Ask HN: Connecting Kubernetes dependencies to application telemetry
author: chipfixer

raw.text:
I’m building Cardinal (cardinalhq.io). One thing that drives me nuts about Kubernetes debugging is the number of steps it takes to go from an application issue to its underlying kubernetes root cause.

Like for example, if I am seeing an error rate spike, and I group by deployment, I want to immediately see the deployment's k8s neighborhood, which would then show me the configmap that was updated recently and incorrectly.

Similarly, say a node is low on disk and that is causing a ripple effect on a statefulset trying to write new files, which then affects request latency.

The list goes on.

To solve this, one idea we had was: build a smart chart legend that recognizes a k8s tag (based on OTEL semantic conventions), and then for every entry pops an "infra map" icon. Click and you see the full k8s neighborhood of that entity with health annotations. So now it's easier to go from app telemetry to k8s infra.

I am curious if this UX makes sense, and if not how do you solve this correlation problem today?

title: Ask HN: Are we normalizing surveillance in the name of safety?
author: dennysora-main

raw.text:
I don’t know if this is just my imagination.

In recent years, I feel like the whole world is slowly moving toward this direction:

“Because we need to protect people, we need to monitor them.”

As a Taiwanese person, I’m very familiar with this kind of logic from the CCP next door.

But for some reason, I feel like more and more of the world is also moving in this direction.

For example:

* Asking an important open-source infrastructure project like Linux to add age verification. * Credit card companies asking Japan to follow all kinds of unreasonable rules. * Using courts to force companies, in the name of human rights or safety, to monitor cloud data. * Requiring VPNs to be controlled or regulated.

These are just some simple examples. I don’t have detailed statistics, but I really feel like there have been more and more cases like this recently.

It is often wrapped in something morally justified, and then surveillance and control are introduced underneath it.

The CCP next door has always used this kind of logic.

Officially, everything is for protection and safety. Encryption is heavily restricted. Whenever these policies are introduced, there are also many people defending them.

Many people do not really feel that their own rights are being violated.

Until one day, the restrictions keep expanding and become something like a censorship system where almost anything can be punished.

On mainland Chinese platforms, if you try to have a deeper discussion about certain topics, or even just ask for opinions, it is very easy to get banned.

Right now, fortunately, there are still many people around the world who keep pushing back against different kinds of surveillance that are packaged as “morally necessary.”

But what I’m afraid of is this:

What if people slowly become used to it?

What if everyone becomes more and more insensitive to these things, like many people in mainland China, and only realizes what happened when almost nothing can be said anymore?

At that point, it may already be too late.

As a side note, the security and identity system in mainland China is basically built more from the perspective of the state.

So you can see many things like:

* A phone number is required almost everywhere. * Email is not used very much. * Communication is mainly through QQ or WeChat. * Passkeys are not common. Most identity verification is based on phone numbers. * Many services look anonymous, but are actually tied to your real identity.

A lot of the “security” mechanisms are related to the state, including speech and political control, rather than the personal security or privacy of the user.

Apps also like to put advertisements everywhere.

One app tries to do everything.

Many apps constantly encourage people to borrow money.

Even on phones and other hardware, anything that allows you to type text may potentially contain blocked words.

Some topics basically cannot be discussed.

Xi Jinping is one obvious example. Even related words or associations, such as “Xi” or Winnie the Pooh, can become sensitive.

China is also very strong in AI, partly because there is so much data and not much privacy.

Sometimes you can see Chinese AI systems that speak in a way that feels very similar to how real people think and talk.

My guess is that this is partly because a lot of real human-to-human conversations have been used for training, including private conversations.

There is probably much more I could add.

But the main point is not really China.

What I am worried about is that one day, even installing Linux on my own computer may require real-name verification.

That kind of thing sounds terrifying to me.

Maybe I’m overthinking it, but I really feel like the direction is becoming more obvious.

I’m curious what people here think.

Do you feel the same way?

Do you think this is actually becoming a broader trend?

title: Ask HN: How safe are our password managers in face of LLM cyber attacks?
author: muddi900

raw.text:
Hey

With LLMs having infinite attack resources compared to human researchers, how safe are we?

We already know that you don't need top tier frontier models to create an attack vector. You can just loop a mid-sized model until it bears result. Or run a small swarm of agents to achieve the same goal

How long until a criminal actor with running exo[1] over 2 mac studios breaches password managers?

I understand that the storage of passwords might be encrypted, but they might find vulnerabilities at the client or transport level.

How may we mitigate this?

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49585683
